Family Health

Hyperthyroidism: where diet and natural remedies fit

Updated: October 7, 2026

Written and edited byMohammadamin Namyar, founder of BeMama: checked against published guidance from recognized health organizations.

An overactive thyroid can affect sleep, mood, weight and the heartbeat, so it is understandable to look for ways to feel better at home. Food and supportive routines can help with daily wellbeing. Supplements need a more careful question: what has actually been studied, for whom, and alongside which medical treatment?

First establish what is causing the hormone excess

Hyperthyroidism means the thyroid is producing too much thyroid hormone. This differs from hypothyroidism, in which there is too little. Graves’ disease, overactive nodules and excess iodine are among possible causes. Thyroid inflammation can release stored hormone through a different process, so a similar set of symptoms does not always call for the same treatment.

Blood tests and the clinical assessment help identify what is happening. A supplement that appears to calm a symptom cannot establish that hormone levels are safe. Before changing food, medicines or herbal products, ask what diagnosis you have and what the treatment is intended to achieve.

Recognize the range of symptoms

An overactive thyroid can cause a fast or irregular heartbeat, tremor, sweating, heat sensitivity, poor sleep, irritability and anxiety. Tiredness, muscle weakness, diarrhea, hair thinning and changes in menstrual periods may occur too. Blood pressure can be affected, and the gland may enlarge into a goitre visible at the front of the neck.

Weight loss often occurs despite an increased appetite, though appetite can vary. Not everyone develops every symptom. These changes can have other causes, so self-diagnosis from a checklist is unreliable. Keep a brief record of the symptoms, their timing and any medicines or supplements you take to help with the assessment.

Medical treatment is individualized

Treatment may involve antithyroid medicine, radioactive iodine or surgery. These are not compulsory steps that everyone follows in the same order. The cause, severity, other health conditions, eye disease and reproductive plans help determine which option fits. A beta blocker may ease a racing heartbeat or tremor while other treatment takes effect.

Feeling calmer does not necessarily mean hormone production is controlled. Keep the prescribed blood-test schedule and discuss how the plan may change over time. After some treatments, thyroid hormone replacement becomes necessary. That is a monitored treatment outcome, not a reason to replace effective care with an unproven remedy.

A low-iodine diet is not the default for everyone

The thyroid needs iodine, but too much can worsen certain thyroid disorders. Avoid starting kelp, seaweed concentrates or iodine drops as a thyroid-health treatment. At the same time, a strict low-iodine diet is not routinely required before every antithyroid prescription and should not be adopted without a specific clinical reason.

The American Thyroid Association’s detailed low-iodine food list is designed for preparation for radioactive iodine treatment for thyroid cancer. Applying it to everyone with an overactive thyroid confuses different treatment situations. If your own team requests temporary dietary restrictions, ask for the exact food guidance and how long it applies.

Understand the food list before removing food groups

Iodized salt, seafood, dairy foods and egg yolks can contribute iodine; bread ingredients and processed foods vary by country and manufacturer. A prescribed preparation diet may also set limits for some grain products or portions of meat. This is not a general instruction to stop eating all bread, pasta, eggs, dairy or meat indefinitely.

Soy products such as tofu and soy milk are not automatically forbidden for every thyroid condition. The frequently cited 2006 review found little evidence of harm in people with normal thyroid function and adequate iodine, while discussing separate concerns about thyroid-medicine absorption. That does not prove a treatment benefit for hyperthyroidism, but it does not support a blanket soy ban either.

Review supplements and hidden sources of iodine

Bring the actual labels of vitamins, herbal blends, weight-loss products and thyroid-support supplements to an appointment. Some contain iodine or multiple active ingredients, and a natural label does not establish safety. Mention nonprescription medicines as well, including products the clinician may not know you use.

Do not stop an essential iodine-containing medicine or change a pregnancy supplement independently. The reason it was prescribed matters. Ask the prescriber to balance thyroid effects with the need for that treatment. Both excessive restriction and excessive supplementation can create problems; the aim is an appropriate intake for your condition.

L-carnitine: a small study is not a universal treatment

L-carnitine is made by the body and is also present in foods such as meat and dairy. Laboratory work suggests it can affect thyroid hormone action in some tissues. A 2001 trial studied 50 women taking a fixed thyroid-hormone dose that suppressed TSH, rather than a broad population with untreated Graves’ disease.

The study reported improvements in several symptoms, but its specific setting does not establish that an over-the-counter product can replace standard treatment. Supplements can cause gastrointestinal effects and may be problematic for people with certain kidney or seizure disorders. Do not assume that being naturally present in food means concentrated doses are harmless.

Bugleweed: limited evidence and uncertain preparations

Bugleweed, also discussed under the botanical name Lycopus, appears in herbal advice for thyroid symptoms. An older three-month open study of Lycopus europaeus reported changes in urinary thyroid-hormone excretion and some symptoms. Its design and patient selection limit what can be concluded about treating clinically significant hyperthyroidism.

Herbs with similar common names may not be the same species, and products differ in concentration and ingredients. Neither a historical use nor a package dosing instruction establishes a safe substitute for antithyroid medicine. Discuss the exact product with the thyroid team before using it, particularly during pregnancy or while taking other medicines.

Vitamin B12 helps when there is a deficiency

Fatigue or weakness can come from thyroid disease, a vitamin deficiency or another condition. Having hyperthyroidism does not automatically mean you are short of vitamin B12. If symptoms or risk factors suggest a deficiency, the clinician can investigate and decide whether replacement is needed.

B12 deficiency may be treated with tablets or injections depending on its cause and severity. Correcting it can improve deficiency-related symptoms but does not treat excess thyroid hormone. A B-complex product is not automatically better. Check all its ingredients and doses rather than treating the phrase B vitamins as a thyroid treatment.

Biotin can interfere with thyroid blood tests

Some B-complex and hair, skin or nail products contain biotin. It can interfere with certain laboratory methods and produce results that look abnormal even when they do not reflect the hormone levels in the body. This is especially relevant when a new supplement is started during thyroid monitoring.

Tell the clinician and laboratory what you take before blood is drawn. Ask how long to withhold a product, if necessary, because the dose and test method matter. Do not interpret an unexpected result or alter prescribed thyroid medicine yourself. A repeat test under suitable conditions may be needed.

Selenium has a narrow role in some thyroid eye disease

Selenium is a mineral found in foods including fish, meat, grains and nuts. It is involved in thyroid biology, but that does not mean everyone with hyperthyroidism should supplement it. Not everyone with Graves’ disease develops thyroid eye disease, and treating the eye condition is a separate question from controlling hormone production.

ATA/ETA guidance allows consideration of a six-month course for selected people with mild active thyroid eye disease, particularly where selenium intake is insufficient. It does not recommend selenium as a universal cure. A 2025 trial in a selenium-sufficient setting found no significant advantage in the main six-month quality-of-life outcome, reinforcing the importance of individual selection.

More selenium is not necessarily safer or better

Excess selenium can cause stomach symptoms, hair or nail changes and other toxicity. Brazil nuts contain high and variable amounts, so a handful is not a precise way to reproduce a clinical dose. Combining a supplement, a multivitamin and deliberate high-selenium eating can increase total intake without making treatment more effective.

If a specialist recommends selenium, confirm the preparation, duration and whether other sources need adjustment. New double vision, reduced vision or other significant eye changes need an eye assessment, not simply a larger supplement dose. Eye symptoms and thyroid blood tests should be followed through the appropriate clinical plan.

Lemon balm is not an established Graves’ treatment

Lemon balm, or Melissa officinalis, is used in teas and herbal preparations. European assessment recognizes traditional use for mild stress, sleep support and digestive symptoms, while noting limited clinical-trial evidence. This does not establish that the herb treats Graves’ disease or reliably controls thyroid hormone levels.

A claim that it works by lowering TSH is also misleading: TSH is often already suppressed when thyroid hormones are excessive. A pleasant tea ritual may feel calming, but that experience is not a hormone test. Discuss concentrated extracts and combination products with a clinician rather than using relaxation as evidence that treatment can be stopped.

Lavender and sandalwood may be comfort choices, not thyroid care

Lavender and sandalwood oils are sometimes promoted for anxiety or sleep. Research on lavender products has important limitations, and evidence for inhaled aromatherapy is uncertain. Results involving a standardized oral product cannot be applied to drinking an essential oil intended for a diffuser. Neither oil is an established treatment for excess thyroid hormone.

If a scent feels relaxing, regard it as a personal comfort measure. Avoid products that trigger coughing, headache or skin irritation, and do not swallow essential oils intended for fragrance. Keep concentrated products away from children. Pregnancy, breastfeeding and interactions require particular care because safety information for many preparations is limited.

Glucomannan was studied as an addition to medicines

Glucomannan is a soluble fiber from konjac root. A small 2007 trial added it to methimazole and propranolol rather than using it instead of those medicines. Some hormone levels fell faster during the early weeks, but the groups did not differ in those levels at eight weeks. This is preliminary evidence about an adjunct, not proof of a standalone remedy.

Fiber supplements can cause bloating or bowel changes and may affect absorption of medicines taken by mouth. Certain tablet preparations have been associated with obstruction in the food pipe. If you are considering a product, ask about its formulation, swallowing safety and medicine timing; do not copy the research regimen from an article.

Food, rest and activity can support recovery

Regular meals and a varied diet can help when appetite, weight and energy needs are changing. Ask for dietetic support if you are losing substantial weight, struggling to eat or avoiding many foods. The practical goal is adequate nutrition alongside treatment, not finding a food that guarantees normal hormone levels.

A calmer bedtime routine, reduced stimulation and support with daily demands may make symptoms easier to manage. Discuss exercise intensity with the team if palpitations, weakness or uncontrolled symptoms are present; pushing through is not a treatment. Keep follow-up even if you feel better, because symptom relief and biochemical control are different measures.

Know when to contact the team urgently

Tell the thyroid team promptly if you become pregnant, are planning pregnancy or are breastfeeding, because treatment choices change. Radioactive iodine is not used during pregnancy or breastfeeding. Do not stop prescribed care on your own; ask for an individualized review and clear instructions about medicines and follow-up.

Fever, a persistent sore throat or jaundice while taking an antithyroid medicine needs immediate medical advice because serious blood-cell or liver problems can occur. Follow the medicine’s urgent side-effect instructions. A very fast heartbeat with high fever, confusion, collapse or severe illness may be a thyroid storm and requires emergency care.

Evidence-informed guidance

What trusted health organizations recommend

NHS, NIDDK and ATA guidance supports cause-specific treatment and review of iodine and supplement exposure. The ATA low-iodine preparation diet addresses a particular thyroid-cancer treatment context; it should not be copied into routine hyperthyroidism advice.

The original L-carnitine and glucomannan studies and an older Lycopus study have limited populations or designs. Selenium recommendations concern selected mild active thyroid eye disease, with a newer selenium-sufficient trial showing no significant primary six-month quality-of-life benefit. None of these findings establishes a general natural cure.

How BeMama can help

Take one list of medicines, supplements and dietary restrictions to the appointment. Ask which item has a clear purpose, which needs monitoring and which adds no demonstrated benefit.

When to seek help

Seek immediate advice for fever, persistent sore throat or jaundice while taking antithyroid medicine. High fever with a very fast heartbeat, confusion or collapse is an emergency. Pregnancy and breastfeeding require an individualized treatment review.

Evidence notes updated: October 7, 2026

Key takeaways

  • Confirm the cause and keep effective treatment and monitoring in place.
  • Avoid excess iodine, but do not impose a strict low-iodine diet without instructions.
  • Correcting B12 deficiency is different from treating hyperthyroidism.
  • Selenium has a specific possible eye-disease role, not a universal thyroid indication.
  • Small supplement studies do not justify replacing prescribed care.

Frequently asked questions

Can food or supplements cure an overactive thyroid?

No diet or supplement discussed here is established as a replacement for cause-specific medical treatment.

Should I stop all dairy, eggs, bread and seafood?

Not automatically. A restrictive preparation diet is for a specific clinical purpose. Ask what your own treatment requires and avoid unnecessarily removing food groups.

Is soy forbidden?

There is no universal ban. Treatment preparation and thyroid-medicine absorption may require specific advice, which is different from saying soy causes hyperthyroidism.

Can I use kelp or iodine drops for thyroid health?

Do not start them for that purpose. Concentrated iodine can worsen some thyroid conditions; discuss the label and your diagnosis with the clinician.

Did the L-carnitine study prove it treats all hyperthyroidism?

No. The 2001 trial involved a small group with thyroid-hormone treatment-related effects. It does not establish broad replacement of standard care.

Should everyone take B12 or a B-complex vitamin?

No. Investigate a suspected deficiency and treat it appropriately. Also disclose biotin, which can interfere with some thyroid blood tests.

Does selenium treat Graves’ disease itself?

It is not a general treatment for excess hormone production. A specialist may consider it for selected mild active thyroid eye disease, depending on circumstances.

Are bugleweed and lemon balm proven thyroid treatments?

No. Limited studies or traditional use do not establish a safe substitute for prescribed treatment. Product identity and interactions matter.

Can I replace thyroid medicine with glucomannan?

No. The small trial studied glucomannan alongside medicines, and an early difference did not persist at eight weeks. It can also affect medicine absorption.

Which symptoms need immediate help?

Contact a clinician immediately for antithyroid medicine-related fever, persistent sore throat or jaundice. High fever with a very fast heartbeat, confusion or collapse needs emergency care.

This article is general education, not medical advice, diagnosis, or treatment. Always talk with a qualified healthcare professional about your situation, and seek urgent care for emergencies.
